    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month.

    A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.

    Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.

    A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman noted that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.

    In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister mentioned the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.

    Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that in a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.

    Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike.

    In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and remarked about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.

    "No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".

    The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.

    The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.

    On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

    Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

    At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

    Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

    The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

    Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry notes.

    Breaking: Character.AI’s plan to auction off customers’ private chats challenged by state AGs

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that what happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt?
    • Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.
    • The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that what happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the proposal is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

    Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

    The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements mentioned.

    Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

    In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, Upcoming York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

    Sources indicate that “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta noted in a statement.

    Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

    Industry observers note that “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong noted. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”.

    Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”.

    The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to customers’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.).

    It has been revealed that character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

    California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

    Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a powerful explosion that rolled out gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.
    • Sources indicate that the detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people.
    • It has been revealed that local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a powerful explosion that rolled out gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.

    Sources indicate that the detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate.

    It has been revealed that local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast.

    Lead is a neurotoxin that does not break down in the environment and poses significant health risks, particularly to young children and pregnant people.

    In the hours leading to the detonation, the Army released maps showing modeled drift and distribution of the plume. They indicated that airborne lead would travel around 100 miles to the southwest of the facility, while dust deposition would cover around 200 square miles in that direction. Researchers and government workers have already collected air and soil samples from the area, which will act as baseline readings for lead levels in the aftermath and fallout of the detonation.

    Industry observers note that in preparation for the blast, the Army surrounded the earth-covered containers with sand-and lime fill. They set up water cannons and misters intended to keep dust down. They also covered the top of the container with fire-suppressant foam. The Army documented the efforts with a video posted to social media Wednesday morning.

    The explosion follows days of confusion, outrage, questions, and delays. Although the Army said that it has known about the hazardous state of the lead azide since March, Iowans were largely unaware of the situation and the planned detonation until last week. At that time, the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on Friday, November 20. But public alarm and an emergency court filing from environmental groups led to a delay, which was initially scheduled for Monday, then Tuesday, and finally to today.

    Sources indicate that A federal appeals court initially issued a stay on the Army’s permit to conduct the detonation, and, on Monday, Trump noted he ordered the military to halt the operation until the court lifted the stay and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat, signed off. Ultimately, the court ruled this week that the Army could move ahead with intends, given no better option.

    But questions continue to swirl about how the lead azide got to such a “catastrophically hazardous condition.” On Tuesday, The Washington Post reported that it had viewed emails that suggest the Army knew since at least September 2025, not this past March.

    It has been revealed that most people probably wouldn't consider a knife to be very techy, and for most blades that sentiment rings true. But on days like Thanksgiving where you're going to be doing a ton of chopping, cutting, slicing and more, it can't hurt to have a little extra help. And then there's the turkey, because it isn't going to carve itself. Furthermore, if you want your bird to look anything like it does in cooking videos with those neat, super clean slices, you're going to need a sharp tool to get there.

    For cooking nerds who like to geek out about the science of sharpness, one of my favorite knives on the market right now is the Seattle Ultrasonics C-200. In addition to just being a really nice knife featuring a three-layer san mai blade made out of Japanese AUS-10 steel, inside its handle there's a motor that vibrates the knife 30,000 times per second. While the oscillations are so small that you can't actually feel it shaking, those vibrations increased the knife's effective sharpness by up to 50 percent. It excels at delicate foods like tomatoes that often like to stick to the side of your blade, but also denser things like potatoes and meat, which obviously includes turkey. The C-200 even comes with an IP65 rating for dust and water resistance, so there's no worry about ruining its electronics with an errant splash. And if you opt for the wireless charging tile, you'll never have to worry about keeping its battery topped up. Granted, starting at $399, it certainly isn't cheap, but that price is very much in the same range as other premium chef knives from significant name companies like Shun, Wusthoff and others.

    Alternatively, if you want a dedicated gadget for helping you carve a turkey, you can always turn to more traditional electric knives like those from Cusinart, NutriChef, Hamilton Beach and more. Admittedly, these types of knives aren't nearly as pretty as blades like the C200 and the need to plug them in makes them harder to use on an everyday basis. But if you want a relatively easy and affordable way to make serving your Thanksgiving turkey go a bit more smoothly, a classic electric knife is definitely worth a look.

    Even if you prefer side dishes like mashed potatoes, stuffing or a green bean casserole, there's no denying that the turkey is the star of Thanksgiving dinner. And if you want it to come out just right, you need a decent thermometer. Not having one is basically gambling that you get lucky with your timing and the bird turns out well. That stated, there are a range of options, from simple digital sticks like the affordable ThermoPop 2 to fancy probe thermometers like the second-gen model from Combustion Inc.

    Basic options require a bit more work as you can't leave them in the bird while it's in the oven, whereas more expensive versions have wireless support that allows you to leave them inside the turkey as it cooks. Some options like those from Combustion Inc. even account for carry-over cooking, which is when the temperature of the food continues to rise even after you take it out of the oven. You just need to decide how much you want to spend and what kind of features you really want. One of my more affordable favorites is the Sense from Chef IQ, which offers a great balance between price and performance. Just don't be a fool and try to rely strictly on the little pop-out thermometers that sometimes come with the bird, as those aren't known for their accuracy or precision.

    Industry observers note that A big issue during Thanksgiving is not having enough room in your oven for everything that needs to be baked or roasted. One easy solution to this is turning to an air fryer, which works almost exactly like the convection function on an oven, but in a smaller volume that's faster to heat and sometimes offers better air circulation. Another really nice thing about air fryers is that they can be quite affordable, with name brand models like the Instant Pot Vortex or the Ninja Air Fryer Pro, both of which are at the moment going for as little as $80.

    Upgrading to more expensive fryers like the Philips 3000 can give you more capacity, while even pricier options like the Wonder Oven Pro from Our Place have as many as eight different functions for things like baking, roasting, dehydrating, proofing and more. And perhaps the best thing is that when the holidays are over, you can easily move these into your pantry, closet or garage and reclaim some of your precious kitchen counter space.

    A good digital scale falls in the same general camp as a decent thermometer and there isn't an experienced baker that would be caught dead without one. They're super easy to use and in my opinion, they are a staple of any well-equipped kitchen. You can just plop a mixing bowl on top, zero out the scale and then add ingredients in as needed while you get precise measurements, which can be especially critical for baked goods and confections. OXO makes a very nice and rather affordable digital scale that starts at around $65, but you can find cheaper options from well-known brands like KitchenAid for barely more than $20.

    In a recent development, A lot of people think blenders are big, bulky contraptions that make a ton of noise and take up too much room in your kitchen. And while the most powerful ones often are, they don't need to be, as there are affordable options that aren't much bigger than a teapot like these ones from Magic Bullet and Ninja. Regardless, they are great for making a post-dinner milkshake or a lovely fall-inspired soup (butternut squash anyone?).

    Industry observers note that alternatively, you can opt for an immersion blender (aka a hand blender), which can do much of the same functions as a big countertop model, but gives you even greater control and the ability to blend things directly on the stovetop using the pots you already own. This can make them better choices for whipping up sauces like hollandaise (which is delicious when poured over roasted asparagus), mayonnaise or even a classic cranberry sauce to go with your turkey. I prefer cordless options like those from KitchenAid as they have more than enough battery life to complete multiple dishes and the lack of a wire makes them super easy to use. But if your budget is tight, traditional cabled options are totally fine too and often a more affordable choice.

    Recent findings suggest that even for people like me who prefer to chop things by hand, a food processor can be an incredible time saver during the holidays. Not only do they make quick minces of veggies, they can also be used to grate cheese, shred things like potatoes (for an easy Thanksgiving hash), or whip up dips like salsa. Some options like the Cusinart Mini Food processor are stupendously cheap at under $30, while pricer models like the Ninja Professional Plus Food Processor come with a bunch of attachments to handle all sorts of dishes.

    Industry observers note that cooking food in a water bath might seem like an unnecessarily complex thing to do for the holidays, but it can actually save you time and effort. A good sous vide machine like those from Anova or Breville allow you to set an exact temperature and hold it there almost indefinitely. This allows you to cook things like meat with precision, so there's no worrying about if something is going to come out medium-rare or well-done.

    And even on Thanksgiving where turkey is the main protein, you can still use a sous vide machine to make dishes like superb rosemary mashed potatoes or luscious glazed carrots. Some models even come with Wi-Fi, so you can start and set them remotely using your phone. On top of that, all they need to function is an outlet, so a sous vide machine can be a great option for people with small kitchens or a limited number of burners on their stove.

    #127543. Is authoritarian Vietnam ready to phase out the death penalty?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1146 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

    Is authoritarian Vietnam ready to phase out the death penalty?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Vietnam, a country once considered one of the world's most prolific executioners, is steadily reducing the number of crimes punishable by death.
    • On November 20, the country's National Assembly approved a revised penal code that abolishes capital punishment for six offenses, including drug trafficking, rape of a person under the age of 16 and crimes against humanity.
    • When the legislation takes effect next March, just four offenses — treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production — will remain punishable by death, down from 44 in 1997.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Vietnam, a country once considered one of the world's most prolific executioners, is steadily reducing the number of crimes punishable by death.

    On November 20, the country's National Assembly approved a revised penal code that abolishes capital punishment for six offenses, including drug trafficking, rape of a person under the age of 16 and crimes against humanity.

    When the legislation takes effect next March, just four offenses — treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production — will remain punishable by death, down from 44 in 1997.

    Although Hanoi has given little indication that it intends to do away with capital punishment entirely, few countries that still regularly execute prisoners have narrowed its legal application so considerably.

    The reforms are particularly striking given that they come as Vietnam's ruling Communist Party has intensified its crackdown on political dissent and independent civil society.

    General Luong Tam Quang, the minister of public security, mentioned the changes reflect humanitarian considerations, the need for more proportionate sentencing and Vietnam's international integration, while maintaining a tough approach to crime, according to the state-run Vietnam News Agency.

    Vietnam's gradual reduction in the number of offenses punishable by death reflects an evolution in its criminal justice philosophy, mentioned Tran Dai Lam, a lawyer at the ANVI law firm in Hanoi.

    "There is a growing recognition that the effectiveness of criminal law depends not necessarily on the severity of punishment, but on the certainty that criminal offenses are detected, prosecuted and punished," he told DW.

    Vietnam's latest reforms come barely a year after the National Assembly abolished the death penalty for eight other offenses, including embezzlement, bribery, espionage and the illegal transportation of drugs.

    The removal of capital punishment for drug trafficking is particularly significant given the prominence of narcotics-related offenses in Vietnam's criminal justice system and the country's proximity to the Golden Triangle, one of the world's largest illicit drug-producing regions.

    The fresh legislation also provides for existing death sentences to be commuted to life imprisonment for offenses that will no longer carry the death penalty.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Hai Luong, a lecturer in criminology at Griffith University in Australia, told DW that Vietnam has been taking a "retentionist-but-reductionist" approach.

    "Vietnam is reforming the death penalty rather than abolishing it," he stated. "The trend is towards a more limited and selective use of capital punishment, but not yet towards its complete removal.".

    According to Luong, the gradual reduction in capital offenses reflects Hanoi's efforts to modernize its legal system without relinquishing its authority to severely punish what it considers the most serious crimes.

    Growing international recognition that capital punishment has little additional deterrent effect is also informing Vietnam's approach, he explained.

    Decades of harsh penalties for drug-related offenses have done little to stem the international narcotics trade, while the continued expansion of drug trafficking networks in Southeast Asia has raised questions about the effectiveness of executions as a crime prevention measure.

    Vietnam's growing integration into the international community, including its participation in international drug control conventions and closer diplomatic ties with Western countries, has also given Hanoi greater incentives to align its criminal justice system with international standards, Luong added.

    Vietnam's gradual retreat from capital punishment could also bring it closer to the European Union on human rights.

    Brussels has repeatedly called on Hanoi to abolish capital punishment, a subject regularly raised during bilateral human rights discussions. The EU, one of the world's most vocal advocates of abolition, has long opposed capital punishment as part of its foreign policy.

    An EU spokesperson told DW that Brussels welcomes "Vietnam's latest reduction in crimes punishable by capital punishment. This is a positive step and shows a disposition to consider gradual reform, leading towards a moratorium first and finally to the abolition of the death penalty.".

    "Any concrete step towards this ultimate goal would be very much welcomed by the EU," they added.

    However, Vietnam's reforms still fall short of international human rights standards, particularly since the death penalty remains available for drug-related offenses that do not involve intentional killing.

    Nor is there much evidence that progress on capital punishment is accompanied by improvements in other areas of Vietnam's human rights record, notably freedom of expression and association.

    It is also difficult to establish whether Vietnam's legislative reforms have resulted in fewer executions.

    Sources indicate that the authorities classify execution statistics as state secrets. Amnesty International believes Vietnam continues to make extensive use of capital punishment, but it cannot provide reliable annual figures.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Vietnam's capital punishment reform allows the state to continue executing people to fulfil its political and public security goals, "while also managing, or massaging, its international reputation through highly publicized 'reductionist' reforms," Daniel Pascoe, an associate professor of law at the City University of Hong Kong and an expert on capital punishment, told DW.

    For example, he added, although the recent abolition of the death penalty for drug trafficking is welcome, "it doesn't tell us whether the Vietnamese authorities will now simply charge a higher number of suspects with the drug production offense, which remains death-eligible.".

    Vietnam's reforms are part of a broader, if uneven, shift away from capital punishment in Southeast Asia.

    Cambodia, the Philippines and East Timor have abolished the death penalty altogether. Malaysia abolished mandatory death sentences in 2023, while Indonesia's latest penal code, which took effect this year, allows for death sentences to be commuted under certain conditions following a 10-year probationary period.

    However, Singapore has increased its use of capital punishment in recent years, particularly for drug-related offenses, while Myanmar's military authorities resumed executions in 2022 after a hiatus of more than three decades.

    Pascoe told DW that although the impact of Vietnam's reforms on execution numbers remains unclear, there is symbolic significance in one of Southeast Asia's most authoritarian governments visibly restricting the death penalty.

    "If a one-party state like Vietnam can reduce the scope of capital punishment, why shouldn't Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Brunei and Myanmar also do so?" Pascoe added.

    The number of countries actively executing people is close to being at an all-time low, but those that are actively executing, such as Iran and Singapore, seem to be increasing their use, Sara Kowal, co-director of Eleos Justice, a research and advocacy initiative against the death penalty at Australia's Monash University, told DW.

    "Vietnam's dramatic reduction of death-eligible offenses is another really positive sign that the global trend towards abolishing the death penalty is continuing," Kowal remarked.

    "It would be great to see Vietnam take the next step to establish an official moratorium on all executions," she added.

    According to Amnesty International, 17 countries carried out executions in 2025, among them China, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the organization could get their encrypted files back.
    • Sources indicate that according to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware.
    • But the manufacturer allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the organization could get their encrypted files back.

    Sources indicate that according to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The manufacturer’s website, which right now reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”.

    But the manufacturer allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

    Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

    Sources indicate that the DOJ stated the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a firm that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

    Recent findings suggest that 404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

    Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

    Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

    The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

    #127538. Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1009 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.
    • Industry observers note that although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China.
    • The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

    Industry observers note that although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.

    The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

    Among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its consumers’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”.

    As the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of Newly introduced York Joseph Nocella Jr. noted that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage firm called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

    One of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ mentioned. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

    Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ said, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade reveals and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The Latest York Times reported.

    Huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ said was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”.

    During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

    Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, remarked that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”.

    Huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the company’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”.

    Sentencing is scheduled for September 14.

    In a recent development, huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”.

    Outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by firm employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”.

    Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”.

    “The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig said.

    It has been revealed that after the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.

    China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo mentioned.

    However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

    Industry observers note that “This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky said. “No company is too significant, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Can you play GTA 6 from an external hard drive on PS5 or Xbox Series X/S?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (295 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rockstar’s behemoth takes up a lot of storage space.
    • Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game of the year by some distance, having racked up $3.79 billion in pre-orders and day-one sales.
    • There will be many other folks who want to play the game and haven't had a chance to jump in yet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rockstar’s behemoth takes up a lot of storage space.

    Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game of the year by some distance, having racked up $3.79 billion in pre-orders and day-one sales. On PlayStation 5 alone, more than 39 million unique players took control of dual protagonists Jason and Lucia on opening weekend, making it the biggest game debut in the 32-year history of PlayStation.

    There will be many other folks who want to play the game and haven't had a chance to jump in yet. One thing they should note is that, with a hefty install size, GTA 6 will take up a significant chunk of their PS5 or Xbox Series X/S storage space.

    You might be wondering whether you can install GTA 6 on an external hard drive to avoid having to delete other games and data from your console. You can move GTA 6 to your external storage when you're not playing it. However, to run the game locally, you'll need to have it installed on your system's built-in storage, an SDD you've installed in your PS5 or a compatible NVMe expansion card that's plugged into your Xbox.

    In a recent development, as with many other recent games, GTA 6 needs to take advantage of the fast-loading capabilities of the PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. The consoles are unable to load data for these titles quickly enough from an external hard drive over a USB connection. For the same reason, disc-based PS5 and Xbox Series X games are installed onto system storage before you can play them. The PS5 can run PS4 games from external storage, though. Likewise, an Xbox Series X/S can run older Xbox One and Xbox 360 titles directly from an external hard drive.

    Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation.

    Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.

    Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.

    A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).

    The organization stated the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.

    Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.

    An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.

    Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

    On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.

    He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any challenges.

    Bangchak Corporation stated air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

    It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The firm has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.

    An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to Latest York kids this Christmas.
    • Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years.
    • The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to Latest York kids this Christmas.

    Sources indicate that gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.

    The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

    Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

    “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”.

    When asked how Newly introduced York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”.

    When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the tech giant said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

    In a recent development, the Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.

    The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules.

    While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.

    According to recent reports, common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors.

    It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January, finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns.

    While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them.

    It has been revealed that “These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.”.

    TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

    Breaking: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers.
    • In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.
    • We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

    In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

    We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

    Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

    The second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

    Industry observers note that much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

    I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

    Such lessons are notable because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki stated:.

    Industry observers note that unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

    Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

    Black Friday isn't quite the major sales event it used to be now that you can get deals multiple times a year through events like Amazon Prime Day, but if you're looking to save this holiday season, there are still some great options.

    Sources indicate that multiple gadgets from Engadget's Best of 2026 list are already on sale, including Samsung's flagship foldable smartphone and Apple's ultra-popular (and cute) entry-level laptop. Online retailers like Amazon seem to offer the steepest discounts, but buying directly from the manufacturer can also net you extra savings, particularly if you have a device you want to trade in. If you don't see what you want on sale now, worry not: Fresh deals will continue to pop up throughout Thanksgiving and Black Friday. In the meantime, here's a selection of what you can save on now.

    Industry observers note that apple has had a big year of product releases, both in terms of wholly newly introduced product categories and old standbys it's finally shown some love. The firm is running its own Black Friday sale on its website through November 30, which can net you Apple gift cards ranging from $25 to $300 depending on the product you purchase, but you can also find some excellent deals on Amazon.

    Recent findings suggest that the colorful new MacBook Neo, Apple's first computer powered by an iPhone chip (the A18 Pro) and its first relatively budget-friendly laptop, is on sale at Amazon for $649, $50 off its normal $699 starting price. The Neo made a big splash when it launched in March because it offered some of the premium benefits of Apple's more expensive computers at an affordable $599, a price Apple unfortunately raised to $699 in June due to the high cost of memory and storage. This discount helps recapture some of that original magic.

    In a recent development, if you'd prefer something more powerful, you can also opt for the upcoming M5 MacBook Air, which is on sale on Amazon for $1,049, $250 off its normal $1,299 price. The new M5 chip is the main upgrade this year, and it offers more than enough power for basic work, with extra headroom for AI tools and light gaming.

    Arguably the best Apple deals so far, though, are the current discounts on the AirPods Pro 3 and the Apple Watch Series 12. You can purchase Apple's high-end wireless earbuds for just $149 on Amazon, a 40 percent discount on the usual $249 Apple charges. Meanwhile, Apple's latest smartwatch — which features a redesigned health sensor — is going for $299 on Amazon, $100 off its normal $399 price.

    Like Apple, Google is offering some exclusive deals on its website if you're interested in saving on accessories or getting an even better deal on a trade-in. The bulk of the company's discounts on smartphones and smartwatches are being reflected across retailers, though.

    For example, both the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro are on sale on Amazon. The base Pixel 11, which comes in fresh colors, includes more storage and has a collection of AI-powered camera features, is on sale on Amazon for $699, over 20 percent off its normal $899 starting price. You can also get the Pixel 11 Pro, Google's higher-end model with its new HiLight customizable notification light, for $749 on Amazon, a $350 discount on its usual $1,099 starting price.

    Industry observers note that if you've already got an Android phone and are looking for a good smartwatch, you can get a Pixel Watch 5, Google's latest smartwatch, on sale on Amazon for $330, $100 off its $430 starting price. The fresh smartwatch offers easy access to Gemini, improved GPS tracking for outdoor workouts and new gestures for controlling the watch without using the touchscreen.

    Sources indicate that while Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, is the hot commodity heading into the holiday season, it doesn't yet have an easy-to-snag Black Friday deal. You can get Engadget's favorite foldable of the year for a healthy discount, though.The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 features a upcoming, more passport-shaped form factor and one of the tech giant's best anti-glare displays. It's also available on Amazon for $1,550, a still eye-popping price, but cheaper than the $1,900 Samsung usually charges. If you're on Android and Duo-curious, the Z Fold 8 is the better foldable anyway.

    For anyone all-in on Gemini and Google's Pixel ecosystem, the less beloved but still competently made Pixel 11 Pro Fold is on sale on Amazon for $1,649. That's a $250 discount on what's usually a $1,899 foldable, and you still get Google's polished take on Android and extensive software support.

    Sources indicate that if you're building out a home office or setting up your first PC gaming rig, you'll want a monitor you're willing to stare at for hours on end. The Alienware 39 5K not only offers ample screen real estate with its 39-inch, ever-so-slightly curved display, but also a wonderfully bright and vivid OLED panel that can switch between 5K 165Hz and 1080p+ 330Hz modes with a button push.

    In a recent development, the monitor is on sale directly through Dell's website for $1,000, $100 off what Dell normally charges. If you want the best experience for gaming and staring at Microsoft Word, it's hard to go wrong with the Alienware 39 5K.

    Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music.

    Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.

    Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

    Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

    Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.

    Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off.

    He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

    Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

    "His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.".

    They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.

    Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".

    Industry observers note that "Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.".

    Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023.

    Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".

    Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix.".

    In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".

    US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".

    Belinda Carlisle stated she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

    Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".

    Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982.

    Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, noted: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together.".

    She noted he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".

    Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs.

    The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

    He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

    The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

    Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

    Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and upcoming wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980s.

    Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.

    Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly debuted MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.

    They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.

    During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.

    The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.

    "We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.

    "We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral.".

    He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.

    Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse Macabre.

    After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

    In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public intends for a reunion.

    When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

    Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

    The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor:.

    Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMT.

    Sounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT.

    Latest York state bans AI chatbot toys for kids

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (480 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Companies violating the five year ban will face a $15,000 per day fine.
    • New York governor Kathy Hochul has signed into law a five-year ban on the sale of AI chatbot toys, including dolls and robots that use the internet to converse with children.
    • Sources indicate that "Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," Hochul mentioned in a statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Companies violating the five year ban will face a $15,000 per day fine.

    New York governor Kathy Hochul has signed into law a five-year ban on the sale of AI chatbot toys, including dolls and robots that use the internet to converse with children. The new law comes with some teeth, including steep daily fines for each violation enforced by the state's attorney general.

    Sources indicate that "Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," Hochul mentioned in a statement. Calling herself New York's first "mom governor," Hochul said the new measure was "deeply personal.".

    Recent findings suggest that the governor's press release cited the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), that tested chatbot toys marketed to children aged three to 12. Some of the toys talked about sexually explicit subjects and provided advice that could create a fire hazard in homes. The toys had few or zero parental controls and the longer the conversation, the more safety limits weakened. Some toys could even record a child's voice or scan their face.

    "AI chatbots in children's toys are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk," said New York attorney general Letitia James.

    Violators face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation, according to the governor's office. James added that her branch would "not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won't allow our children's health to become the collateral damage of big tech.".

    Hochul and Newly introduced York State legislators recently enacted another law called "AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors," prohibiting unsafe chatbot features for children under 18, with civil penalties of up to $25,000 per infraction. Hochul also signed an executive order this summer, issuing a one-year ban data centers using 50MW or more.

    It has been revealed that anti-AI measures were a politically popular during US midterm elections, as Americans voted to restrict the country's data center boom. Data centers were the subject of 45 ballot measures in 10 states and 39 measures were passed to restrict the facilities in some form.

    In a statement, Amazon remarked the products it sells must follow US laws. "We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations," Amazon told NBC News. "Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families. We support efforts across the industry and government to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops." However, the retail giant sells some 12 million different toys in the US (as of 2023), so complying with the NY AI chatbot law could be a tall order.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s upcoming AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

    In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the manufacturer’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.

    Industry observers note that “Our recent terms revision was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

    Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the manufacturer had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

    He said he still aims on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

    According to recent reports, “I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he noted. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

    He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

    “This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

    The fracas began earlier this month, when the company first proposed latest contractual language. The updated terms read:.

    As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

    Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

    Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

    “Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the company’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

    For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
    • The Toronto-based tech company stated in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.
    • According to recent reports, the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the tech giant’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

    The Toronto-based tech company stated in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

    According to recent reports, the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the tech giant’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company remarked that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

    1Password noted that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The firm also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

    In addition, the organization noted that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

    It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

    Industry observers note that 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll upgrade if we hear back from 1Password.

    The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.
